chief_complaint: Pain in the right upper abdomen and a feeling of faintness.
history_of_present_illness: The patient began experiencing a feeling of fullness in his upper abdomen 1 month prior to admission. In the week before admission, he developed pain in the right upper abdomen, particularly when sleeping on his right side, and recently started to feel breathless on lying down and faint, especially on standing up. Three years previously, he had a blistering and painful skin lesion on the right side of his abdomen around the umbilicus that healed spontaneously.
exposure_and_epidemiology: Patient is from Malawi, where tuberculosis is the most common cause of pericardial effusion and there is a strong association between tuberculosis and HIV infection. A past history of a blistering and painful skin lesion (likely herpes zoster) strongly points to HIV infection.
vitals: Pulse was regular at 130 bpm with a pronounced pulsus paradoxus measured at 15 mmHg. Blood pressure in the supine position was 90/60 mm Hg.
physical_exam: The patient was thin and slightly breathless in the supine position. The jugular venous pulse was elevated, and the apex beat was impalpable. Heart sounds were quiet but audible, with no triple rhythm or murmurs. Auscultation of the chest was normal. An enlarged tender palpable liver was measured at 8 cm below the right costal junction, and there was mild peripheral oedema of the legs and sacral area.
labs_and_diagnostics: Haemoglobin was 10.5 g/dL; WBC was 9.8 G/L (4–10). A chest radiograph showed an enlarged globular heart with clear lung fields. An HIV test was positive. An ultrasound of the heart would show pericardial fluid and possibly fibrous strands. An ECG might show low-voltage QRS complexes or electrical alternans.
differential_diagnosis: Pericardial tamponade caused by a large pericardial effusion. Causes considered in Africa include tuberculosis, other bacterial infections, malignancy, and HIV-related Kaposi's sarcoma. HIV-associated tuberculosis was deemed the most likely diagnosis given the history of herpes zoster.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient underwent therapeutic pericardial aspiration, with 500 mL of bloodstained pericardial fluid aspirated, leading to an immediate increase in blood pressure to 120/80 mmHg. He was started on standard first-line antituberculous treatment (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) daily, along with prednisolone 60 mg daily. After confirmation of HIV-positive status, antiretroviral therapy was started 4 weeks after commencing antituberculous treatment. He received a full 6-month course of antituberculous treatment and prednisolone in tapering doses for 10 weeks, resulting in a full and uneventful recovery.
final_diagnosis: HIV-associated tuberculous pericardial effusion with cardiac tamponade.
